submission.natural_language_explanation: The pole fires at the point where a text commits to a specific amount, measure or target: on numerals and on the punctuation, scale words and unit nouns inside quantity expressions (decimal points, thousands groups, 'million'/'thousand'/'hundred', 'percent', 'metres'/'feet'/'years'), on the bracket that opens a metric equivalent or gloss after a term ('8 inches (200 mm)', 'Minoxidil (Rogaine)'), on months inside dates, and on the 'to'/'in' that introduces the target or time of an orientation, response or suitability predicate (appeal/cater/speak/attend/respond/adapt + to, due in, intended/tailor-made for). It stays quiet on vague quantifiers (many, several, very), on plain counts inside a narrative frame ('there were 30 people in the room', 'the meeting lasted 30 minutes'), and on reference or motion 'to' ('refer to the rules', 'walked to the store').

Federal Energy Regulatory Commission
Division of Dam Safety and Inspections
Report of Periodic Inspection

On the morning of the inspection the weather was overcast with intermittent drizzle, and the surface of the reservoir was calm. The inspection team met the project engineer at the gatehouse and reviewed the operation and maintenance records for the preceding twelve months. The records were complete, legible, and consistent with the monitoring data supplied by the automated instrumentation network. No unapproved modifications to the project works were noted during the document review, and the licensee's staff answered every question the team raised.

The team then walked the crest from the left abutment to the right abutment, checking for settlement, cracking, seepage, and excessive vegetation. The parapet wall appeared sound, although several sections of the railing showed minor surface corrosion where the galvanized coating had worn away. Vegetation on the downstream slope had been mowed as required by the maintenance plan, and no evidence of burrowing animals was observed. The crest road drains were clear and discharged freely.

At the spillway the team examined the concrete chute, the radial gates, and the stilling basin. The gates operated smoothly through a full test cycle, and the gate position indicators in the control room matched the physical positions observed at the structure. The concrete surfaces showed isolated hairline cracks, none of which appeared to be active or to penetrate deeply into the section. In the lower chute, however, the team observed a horizontal crack that extended across roughly two thirds of the slab and appeared wider than it had been at the previous inspection. A crack gauge installed during a later site visit recorded a maximum opening of 0.8 millimetres at the center of the affected span. That reading exceeds the threshold of 0.5 millimetres given in the agency's engineering guidelines, and the crack should therefore be treated as a deficiency requiring evaluation by a qualified structural engineer.

The team recommends that the licensee retain an independent consultant to determine the cause of the cracking and to design an appropriate repair. Until that evaluation is complete, the licensee should monitor the crack on a monthly schedule, record any further movement, and report the readings to the regional office. Drainage near the right abutment also deserves attention. A small pool of standing water was present near the toe of the downstream slope, which may indicate a clogged toe drain or a localized zone of high permeability in the foundation soils.

Nothing observed during this inspection suggested an immediate threat to the safety of the dam or to the downstream community. The deficiencies described above are maintenance items and should be corrected within the timeframes specified in the agency's guidelines. A follow-up inspection will be scheduled to confirm that the recommended repairs have been completed and that no new deficiencies have developed. The licensee should submit a written response describing the actions taken within sixty days of receiving this report.
